headline: The Sabah claim that won't die: what Malaysia won, and what no court has settled
context: The Philippines reaffirmed its Sabah sovereignty claim in February 2026. Malaysia has won every court case (Paris, The Hague, Netherlands), all on procedure. No court has ruled on the 1878 'ceded vs leased' question, because Malaysia has never consented to ICJ jurisdiction.

changes.summary: Correction: this card split the 2013 toll into 68 militants and 10 security personnel and said payments had run since 1963; Malaysia's official Sulu case portal records 78 casualties and says the attack ended the payments.

cards.big: The Philippines still claims Sabah. Malaysia has won every court case. None has ruled on the core question: sale or lease?
cards.sub: In February 2026, the DFA reaffirmed sovereignty after a NAMRIA map showed Sabah as Philippine territory. Every Malaysian win (Paris, The Hague, Netherlands) was procedural.

cards.big: One word, 'ceded' or 'leased', in an 1878 document has generated 148 years of dispute. No court has been asked to rule on it.
cards.sub: English says cede. Sulu text says pajakkan (lease). RA5446 (1968) preserves the claim. No Philippine president dares repeal it.

cards.big: In 2013, armed followers of a Sulu claimant invaded eastern Sabah: 78 casualties, by Malaysia's count. The claim has produced armed incursion within living memory.
cards.sub: Malaysia's official Sulu case portal says the attack prompted it to end the annual cession payments.

cards.big: Sabah unanimously rejects the claim. But 810,000 foreigners, 23.7% of the population, live in the space between two nations' arguments.
cards.sub: Statelessness, birth barriers and healthcare exclusion affect Filipino-descent families. Bajau Laut homes were demolished in Semporna in 2024.

cards.big: The real question is not who owns Sabah. Self-determination and 63 years of statehood answer that. It is why two nations keep a 148-year dispute alive.
Malaysia wins on law. The Philippines loses on law. The people who pay (stateless families, border communities) have no seat at either table.
